title: How the metre was defined in the 1790s by measuring the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona

facts.text: Before the French Revolution, France used up to about 800 different units of measurement.
Counting local variations, one historian puts the number of measures used in France before the revolution at about 250,000.
The same unit could differ from town to town: a pinte held 0.93 liters in Paris but 1.46 liters in nearby Saint-Denis.
Some old units were vague; a cloth measure depended on the width of local looms.
The confusion made cheating easy and got in the way of trade inside France and with other countries.
Scientists rejected simply making the measures of Paris the national standard, seeing them as arbitrary.
In 1790 the Academy of Sciences set up a commission on weights and measures; in March 1791 it proposed a new unit of length.
The metre was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian through Paris.
The idea was to base the unit on nature so that it would belong to no single town or country and other nations might accept it.
Astronomers Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain began measuring the meridian in 1792.
They measured the stretch from Dunkirk on France's north coast through Paris to Barcelona in Spain, then worked out the rest of the pole-to-equator distance.
Delambre took the longer northern part (Dunkirk to Rodez); Méchain took the southern part (Rodez to Barcelona).
They used triangulation, measuring the angles between survey stations (some on mountain peaks) with Borda's repeating circle.
The surveyors worked through disease and revolutionary violence; war between France and Spain in 1793 forced Méchain to stop work in Barcelona.
Méchain found that two sets of his latitude readings for Barcelona did not agree, kept it secret, and later altered some figures.
After Méchain's death, Delambre found the problem but, since the metre was already law, he kept it hidden.
The fieldwork was finished in 1798, roughly six years after it began; the whole task is often described as a seven-year journey.
The resulting metre turned out to be about 0.2 millimeters shorter than one true ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance.
In 1799 a platinum bar was made as the definitive metre, replacing a provisional standard; France officially adopted the system on December 10, 1799.
Many people kept using the old measures, and Napoleon allowed a compromise system with traditional names in 1812.
In 1837 France restored the metric system and dropped the old and compromise measures.
Full adoption of the metric system around the world took more than 100 years.
In 1889 the metre was redefined by an international prototype bar of platinum-iridium.
In 1960 the metre was redefined using the wavelength of light given off by krypton-86 atoms.
Since 1983 the metre has been the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Today only the United States, Liberia and Myanmar have not officially switched to the metric system.
Derived: the 1983 definition came 192 years after the 1791 proposal to base the metre on the size of the Earth.
